source.excerpt: Make your ego porous. Will is of little importance, complaining is nothing, fame is nothing. Openness, patience, receptivity, solitude is everything.
trail: Wikiquote's Rilke page ↗ lists the line in its main Quotes section — not among misattributed or disputed material — with a single citation: “As quoted in Sunbeams: A Book of Quotations (1990) by Sy Safransky, p. 42.” That anthology is the whole of the documentation.

Sunbeams ↗ is a 176-page quotation collection published by North Atlantic Books in 1990 and compiled by Sy Safransky, who founded and edits The Sun ↗; a revised edition followed in 2012. It records who said a thing, not where.

Downstream, the trail thins rather than thickens. Goodreads ↗ attaches no book at all, and The Quotations Page ↗ lists it under “Contributed Quotations” — i.e. submitted by a reader. Quote Investigator has never published on it.

We also checked the eight German Rilke volumes hosted at Project Gutenberg ↗ — Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge, Das Stunden-Buch, both parts of Neue Gedichte, Das Buch der Bilder, Erste Gedichte, Das Marien-Leben and Auguste Rodin. The word porös occurs in none of them. That is not proof of absence — Rilke's correspondence, the likeliest home for a sentence like this, is not on Gutenberg — but it rules out the published books most often assumed to be the origin.
source.excerptNote: Printed everywhere as a free-standing aphorism. No surrounding passage exists in the record — there is no letter, chapter or paragraph it has ever been shown to sit inside.

sourceLink.text: Sunbeams: A Book of Quotations (1990) at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because neither the work nor the translator is known. Rilke died in 1926 and his German books published before 1931 are in the public domain in the United States — but an English translation carries its own copyright, and this English wording's author, date and publisher have never been identified. Nothing here supports calling the sentence public domain.

author.name: Rainer Maria Rilke
author.kicker: The poet it is credited to
author.heading: Rainer Maria Rilke
author.metaLine: 1875–1926 · Austrian poet & novelist who wrote in German
author.bio: Born in Prague in 1875 and dead at Montreux in 1926, Rilke wrote the Duino Elegies, the Sonnets to Orpheus and The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge — but his widest modern fame rests on a book he never assembled. Letters to a Young Poet collects ten letters he sent the cadet Franz Xaver Kappus between 1902 and 1908, published posthumously in 1929, and it is the reason Rilke is quoted more often as a counsellor than as a poet. That reputation is precisely what makes his name a magnet: a calm imperative about solitude and patience sounds like him whether or not he wrote it.

misattribution.heading: Nobody else claims it — and nobody can place it
misattribution.intro: This is not the usual misattribution, where a rival author turns up holding the receipt. No one else is credited with the line. The defect is at the other end: in thirty-five years of circulation, not one reference work has named the Rilke text it came out of.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line with exactly one citation — “As quoted in Sunbeams: A Book of Quotations (1990) by Sy Safransky, p. 42”. That is a record of where the line was reprinted, not where it was written; the anthology names Rilke but no work, letter, date or translator.

items.who: Goodreads, The Quotations Page and the rest
items.why: Goodreads ↗ carries only “— Rainer Maria Rilke” under the text, with topic tags and no book. The Quotations Page ↗ files it under “Contributed Quotations” — a reader submission, offered with no provenance whatever.

German quote sites do carry a German version — “Mach dein Ego porös. Wille ist von geringer Bedeutung…” ↗ — but with no Quelle, and it uses the loanword Ego where Rilke's German would have reached for Ich. Our reading is that the German was made from the English rather than the other way round, which is the ordinary signature of a line that began life in English.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest state of the record: consistently credited to Rilke, entirely at home among his themes, and traceable no further back than a 1990 book of quotations ↗. Until someone produces the letter, treat it as attributed — not as a documented Rilke sentence.

context.heading: Why it sounds exactly like him
lead: Rilke spent six years writing to a young army cadet, Franz Xaver Kappus, telling him to stop asking other people whether his poems were any good. Those ten letters, written between 1902 and 1908 and published posthumously in 1929 ↗, made solitude and patience the two words most people now associate with his name — which is why a sentence ranking “openness, patience, receptivity, solitude” above will, complaint and fame reads as unmistakably Rilkean.

That resemblance is the whole difficulty. A line that sounds like an author is the hardest kind to check, because nobody stops to ask where it came from. This one has travelled through quotation books, greeting cards and social feeds for more than three decades without anyone producing the page it was copied from.
context.detailsSummary: Why an anthology citation is not a source
detailsBody: Quotation anthologies answer a different question from the one a provenance check asks. Sunbeams tells you who is said to have said a thing; it does not tell you which book, letter or lecture it was lifted from, and it does not identify the translator — which for a German-language poet is the decisive detail, since the English wording is somebody's choice, not Rilke's.

Once a line enters a popular anthology it acquires a citation that looks authoritative and travels indefinitely. Every later database here cites Sunbeams, or cites a site that cites Sunbeams, or cites nothing at all. The chain is long, but it is one link deep.
context.pull: Traceable to 1990. Not, so far, to Rilke.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Rainer Maria Rilke page lists the quote in its main Quotes section with the sole citation "As quoted in Sunbeams : A Book of Quotations (1990) by Sy Safransky, p. 42", and does not place it under Misattributed or Disputed.
Sunbeams: A Book of Quotations by Sy Safransky was published by North Atlantic Books in 1990 and runs 176 pages.
The Quotations Page gives no source for the quote and files it under "Contributed Quotations", indicating a reader submission.
Goodreads carries the quote with only the author line "― Rainer Maria Rilke" and topic tags, naming no book or source.

German quote sites carry the wording "Mach dein Ego porös. Wille ist von geringer Bedeutung, Klagen ist nichts, Ruhm ist nichts. Offenheit, Geduld, Empfänglichkeit, Einsamkeit ist alles." with no Quelle (source) given.

Rilke was born 4 December 1875 in Prague and died 29 December 1926 in Montreux; Letters to a Young Poet collects ten letters written between 1902 and 1908 to Franz Xaver Kappus and was published posthumously in 1929.
Sy Safransky founded The Sun magazine in 1974 and edits it; the article's anthologies list includes Sunbeams: A Book of Quotations Revised Edition (2012).

Project Gutenberg hosts Rainer Maria Rilke's works, including Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge, Das Stunden-Buch, Neue Gedichte, Das Buch der Bilder, Erste Gedichte, Das Marien-Leben and Auguste Rodin.
LibQuotes repeats the same single citation for the quote, "As quoted in Sunbeams : A Book of Quotations (1990) by Sy Safransky, p. 42", naming no Rilke work.
